title: Films that aren't necessarily "problematic" but came out at a strange time?

commenti.body:
Isn’t it better than in the past where women often were characters that didn’t matter?

They would show up for a few scenes or even a large part of the movie. They would never have a finished arc and just disappear or fade in the background. They would just be a vehicle for the male lead in one way or the other.

That is such a common trope in a lot of movies. One of my favorite Scorsese films is Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore. He made a great movie with a female lead. He did his best to understand his lead and worked closely with Ellen Burstyn to get the character right. 

I think this weird gatekeeping of movies are incredibly destructive and doesn’t add anything. Trying to equate the plot of a movie to Me Too is just poisonous to me.

I mean if you're reducing both of those movies into that interpretation, sure? But, I think they're much more nuanced and compelling, with some devastating performances. I think it's unfair to demand directors who are women to have to tell those stories. While I recognize the historic disenfranchisement of women and people of color from positions of power in Hollywood, I want to hear stories they want to tell. EEAAO was a gripping story about mother-daughter trauma, is there any consensus that the Daniel's shouldn't have done that and made it a Father-Son relationship instead?   


I had a similar question to your post about The Last Duel by Ridley Scott; I wasn't sure if he was the right person to tell that story. I'm glad I was wrong and think it's one of his most surprising and interesting works in a decade. He had an extremely compelling screenplay and talented actors to help tell a story that could have been done terribly. I think the gender of a director doesn't necessarily matter if they have a strong production team, great respect and communication with their actors, and the professional working conditions actresses have demanded since MeToo (i.e. intimacy coordinators on set).   


The main complaint I have about it coming out at "a strange time" is that everyone flattens these movies into being called problematic and into this binary culture war context, which is extremely disingenuous.

I dont really agree. While yes it might be an awkward time it is important to show how power dynamics can be hateful regardless of gender. There were female slave owners in history who were incredibly cruel, there were female heads of state and royalty who were cruel and sanctioned the deaths of countless people and the destruction of indigenous lands across the world, there were and are women who fight to maintain horrible systems that oppress marginalized people around the world.

Women are human beings and all people can be cruel and commit evil when they are in positions of power over others. It is important to have movies that explore that fact if we are to truly say that not only are men and women equal intrinsically (they are) but also that the real any are systems that allow abuses of power and that create disparities of power between individuals regardless of what it is(race, gender, age, ethnicity, religion, etc)

Lastly dont forget the intersectional aspects of these films. What kind of women have the power? Why are they able to act this way? Why does society reward them over others? These are real world questions many people (men and women) in marginalized positions must ask. Especially when they are on the receiving end of said abuse(I know from experience lol)

I haven't seen May December yet, but I have seen Tár, and I think it's unfair to critique it as a "women can be abusers too" movie, though I am sympathetic to the concern. I am also critical of the idea that it was "made by a man," as if Cate Blanchett contributed nothing to the character -- Todd Field is on record saying that he would never have made the film without her. We must be mindful that movies are collaborative.

That said, I think the choice of a lesbian as the protagonist was deliberate, not to focus on "women, too," but actually to avoid the topic of gender in general. If Tár was a man, then it would just be a "men suck" film, which isn't a difficult point to make so soon after #MeToo. Rather, by placing Tár as both a woman and declining to make her hetero, it puts the focus instead on her ambition, her self-made cult of personality, and, obviously, her egregious abuse of power when in a position of immense influence -- essentially, all the factors that lead to a Harvey Weinstein-type situation. It becomes a much more fascinating character study than if it was just "men are sexual deviants and women only ever helpless victims." That's not a character study anymore, that's just a broader and self-righteous film that would work with a wider audience, but would offer less insight into the complexities of power and psychology. It's what differentiates Tár from a movie like Promising Young Woman, which is more of a revenge tale about gender dynamics, rather than a character study.

None of this, however, is to say that Tár shouldn't be heavily examined and critiqued by feminist and queer perspectives. Even with the best of intentions, that Tár casts a queer woman as the central character will still lend it to interpretations, especially by biased and bigoted audiences, that there's something essential about queerness in the abuse that Tár enacts on her victims. So I do actually think your inquiry, as well as the already existent commentary on the choice of a lesbian for the character of Tár, still serve an important purpose. Todd Fields, as a man, as well as Cate Blanchett, as a straight woman, can only do so much to account for the full experience of a queer woman. Critique is prudent, and this discussion, I believe, is productive.

Currently, only 22% of working directors are women. If you want female-led movies to be made by women, you’re asking that only 22% of movies be about female characters. Is that what you want? If not, you should probably be asking for more gender representation behind the camera before demanding the demographics of lead characters in fictional movies line up with the director of the movie.

Tar and May December are some of the best films of the 21st century. They both have incredible portrayals of interesting, complex, and terrible women. The idea that male filmmakers can't make interesting movies about women is bizarre to me.

Well I suppose that's a source of the problem isn't it? I don't think I said anything to deny that? I pointed out a symptom: that so many of the biggest female character studies are made by men, and my opinion: that I wish more films like this were made by women. I agree that there needs to be more gender representation behind the camera. That's the problem. 

No I do not think that we should have less movies about female characters or that male directors shouldn't be allowed to make them. That was never something I meant to communicate.

Where did I say male filmmakers can't make interesting movies about women? While I have rethought a lot of what I said in my post (explained briefly in my edit) I really think this is getting misinterpreted. I would love to see more female representation behind the camera. I would love to see more of these character studies being made by women. I do not however think that these films shouldn't be made by men, at most it just seems like a majority of the biggest ones are made by men.

Why is there a harm that these films are made by men? They're obviously not exclusively made by men. Are you seriously arguing that men do not have the right to make these sorts of films or are in some way stepping on the toes of female filmmakers by making them?
I am saying that I'd love to see more gender representation behind the camera.
...why is this harmed by tar and may december being made by men?
I didn't say it's harmed by tar and may december being made by men. That has never been my point, if you think it is then you have misunderstood.

I think on contrary: in such times works like that are needed.

Because human has tendency to think about world simplified way,  that's make our life easier. Cofrontation with situations which don't go along with our imagination of issue maybe it is unpleasant but it is very important. Unfortunately social network let us live today in dreamland, where we can make opinion based not on facts but on fantasies which matches with our point of view. And this is very dangerous things for society because it creates bubbles which members don't know much about real world.

Your post was more about the symptom of the issue than the issue itself then. It just seemed odd to single out Todd Field and Todd Haynes for creating stories with complex female leads when your actual issue lies with a completely different aspect of the film industry entirely.
"It just feels like a weird time to have male filmmakers be making women can be abusers too movies" I do not know how to interpret this other than a criticism of those films being made by men.
Yes, it was my goal to point put the symptom of the issue than the issue itself. If you don't think that's productive I understand, I've already deleted the post.
